title: AI Knowledge Management and Content Governance

questions.question: Why do AI assistants need governed knowledge sources?
options: Because content owners are never needed once a document is uploaded to the assistant
Because retrieval can make stale or wrong sources look authoritative and trustworthy
Because access rules should be ignored so retrieval can search everything freely
Because duplicate answers across sources actually improve user trust in the assistant
questions.explanation: Retrieval can surface a stale or wrong source and present it as authoritative — content owners still matter, access rules still apply, and duplicate answers undermine trust rather than improving it.

questions.question: Two SharePoint pages give contradictory instructions for the same expense-approval process, and the assistant sometimes cites one page and sometimes the other. Which of the lesson's four signals does this match most directly?
options: Duplicate answer — conflicting versions of the same content exist and haven't been reconciled
Stale content — the page hasn't been updated even though the process it describes has changed recently
Unclear source — no one can tell which document is the authoritative one to cite
Access risk — the page is visible to people who shouldn't be able to read it
questions.explanation: Two contradictory pages describing the same process is the lesson's duplicate-answer signal — distinct from stale content (outdated but singular), unclear source (no clear authoritative origin), or access risk (wrong visibility).

questions.question: What does the Python artifact produce?
options: A ranked content-governance readiness plan with controls for each source
A complete, fully populated knowledge base ready to connect to an assistant
An access-control server that manages permissions across every content source
A finalized governance policy document ready for executive sign-off
questions.explanation: The artifact ranks source risks into a content-governance readiness plan with controls — it doesn't build a knowledge base, stand up an access-control server, or finalize a policy.

questions.question: Which control belongs to this lesson?
options: Ignoring source rank so every document is treated as equally authoritative
Freshness check — confirming a source still reflects the current process
Removing content owners once a document has been indexed for retrieval
Skipping the access review so retrieval can reach every document by default
questions.explanation: The lesson's controls are content owner, freshness check, source rank, and access rule — freshness check confirms a source still matches the current process, unlike ignoring rank, removing owners, or skipping access review.

questions.question: When should content be cleaned up before AI use?
options: Only when nobody in the organization is actively using the content anymore
When content is stale, duplicated, ownerless, or sensitive from an access standpoint
Only when the content has already passed a full editorial and legal review
Never — retrieval quality alone is enough to fix source-quality problems
questions.explanation: Stale, duplicated, ownerless, or access-sensitive content is exactly when cleanup is needed before AI use — not only unused content, already-reviewed content, or trusting retrieval to fix source quality.

questions.question: What should every important knowledge source have?
options: A named owner, a freshness check, a source rank, and a clear access rule
No review date, since freshness matters less than completeness for AI sources
Unlimited access for every employee, since access rules slow retrieval down
Conflicting duplicates left unresolved, since AI can pick the better version itself
questions.explanation: Every important source needs a named owner, a freshness check, a source rank, and an access rule — not an absent review date, unlimited access, or unresolved duplicates left for AI to sort out.
